en: Cariyāpiṭaka, Akittivagga, Dānapāramī 2: The Perfection of Giving, Story 2. Long ago, O monks, when humans lived for forty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Atthadassī, an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and men, a Buddha, and a Blessed One. He dwelt surrounded by a community of twelve hundred thousand bhikkhus in Bandhumatī, the royal capital. At that time, O monks, King Bandhumant was ruling over the kingdom of Bandhumatī. He was virtuous, a righteous king who protected his subjects righteously; he was beloved and dear to the people, including the brahmins and householders of the countryside. He was handsome, pleasing to behold, graceful, and possessed of supreme beauty. Now, O monks, King Bandhumant had a daughter named Pabhāvatī. She was beautiful, fair to behold, graceful, and possessed of supreme beauty. She was endowed with all the marks of a woman. Then, O monks, King Bandhumant addressed his ministers thus: "Come, sirs, go to the park and see if you can find a maiden endowed with such beauty as my daughter Pabhāvatī. "Yes, sire," those ministers replied to King Bandhumant, and having gone to the park, they searched for a maiden endowed with such beauty as Pabhāvatī. While searching, they saw a daughter of a certain brahmin family who was endowed with such beauty as Pabhāvatī. They informed the king: "Sire, this daughter of a certain brahmin family is endowed with such beauty as Pabhāvatī. Then, O monks, King Bandhumant sent a messenger to that brahmin, saying: "Let this daughter of yours be given to me as a wife for my son. The brahmin replied: "Sire, she is not fit to be a wife for your son; rather, she is fit to be a wife for your majesty yourself. A second and a third time, O monks, King Bandhumant sent the same message, and each time the brahmin gave the same reply. Then, O monks, King Bandhumant went to that brahmin himself and said: "Let this daughter of yours be given to me as a wife for my son. The brahmin replied: "Sire, she is not fit to be a wife for your son; rather, she is fit to be a wife for your majesty yourself. King Bandhumant said: "If it is so, let her be given to me as a wife for myself. The brahmin replied: "Sire, if it is so, let her be given. Then, O monks, King Bandhumant took the brahmin’s daughter as his own wife. Not long after, she conceived a child in her womb. When the ten months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son. Because he was born from the womb of a queen, he was named Prince Mahāpanāda. When Prince Mahāpanāda reached the age of seven, O monks, King Bandhumant addressed his ministers thus: "Come, sirs, go to the park and see if you can find a maiden endowed with such beauty as my son Mahāpanāda. King Bandhumant said: "If it is so, let her be given to me as a wife for myself. The brahmin replied:
In another birth,
when I was a brahmin named Saṅkha:
Desiring to cross the great ocean,
I approached a port. There,
on the path before me, I saw—
The Self-Existent One, unconquered,
was traveling through a wilderness on a journey,
upon a ground that was hot and hard.
Seeing him on the opposite path,
I reflected on this matter:
"This field has been reached."
For a person desiring merit,
just as a farmer, having seen a field like a great village;
Therein, one who does not sow the seed has no need for grain;
even so am I, desiring merit.
Having seen this most excellent field,
if I do not perform an act of merit therein,
I shall have no need for merit.
Just as a minister, desiring his own power,
does not give wealth or grain to the people in the king's inner palace;
Having been delighted, he falls away.
In the same way, I, desiring merit,
having seen a vast sacrificial gift—
‘If I do not give him this gift,
I shall fall away from merit.
Having thought thus, I—
Having descended, I took off my sandals;
having bowed at his feet,
I gave him the parasol and the sandals.
For that very reason,
being delicate and nurtured in comfort,
I was a hundredfold more so; yet even thus, I fulfilled my generosity.
"In this way they gave it to him.
This is the second chapter on the conduct of Saṅkha.
